title: Beyond capillary condensation: Shear-induced bridging transitions in patterned slits
authors: Alexandr Malijevský, Andrew O. Parry, Jiří Janek
abstract: We study the equilibrium phase behavior of a fluid confined in a slit made from two patterned walls. Shearing the walls frustrates the fluid, due to a competition between capillary condensation and interface delocalization, forcing the formation of bridging phases with different pinning properties. This leads to an unusually rich phase diagram, displaying first-order and continuous phase transitions, depending sensitively on the slit width and shear. Generalized Kelvin equations determine the phase boundaries, while the bridging phases are characterized by large correlation lengths, predictions for which are tested using a microscopic density functional model.
summary: This work theoretically maps the complex phase diagram of a fluid confined between patterned walls subjected to shear. The competition between capillary condensation and interface delocalization forces the formation of novel 'bridging phases.' The research uses generalized Kelvin equations and DFT to predict multiple types of phase transitions, providing detailed insights into how geometry and external fields dictate fluid behavior.
main_problem: The study investigates the equilibrium phase behavior of a fluid confined within a slit formed by two patterned walls, focusing on the complex transitions induced by external shear.
main_result: The competition between capillary condensation and interface delocalization leads to an unusually rich phase diagram featuring multiple bridging phases (Type I, IIA, IIB, III) and both first-order and continuous phase transitions.
method: The analysis employs generalized Kelvin equations to determine phase boundaries, supplemented by a microscopic density functional model (DFT) to characterize the bridging phases.
model_or_system: The system is a fluid confined in a slit with patterned walls exhibiting competing wetting properties, subjected to a lateral shear displacement. The theoretical framework utilizes the grand potential ($\Omega$) calculated from surface tensions.
key_observables: Phase identification (CG, CL, bridging phases), phase transition types (first-order/continuous), and the correlation length ($\xi_y$) within the bridging phases.
important_parameters: Slit width ($L$), shear displacement ($\delta$), and the wetting contrast ($	heta$). Specific regimes are defined by comparing $L$ and $\delta$ against critical widths like $L_T(\delta)$ and $L_D(\delta)$.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on macroscopic descriptions corrected by mesoscopic terms (e.g., logarithmic corrections to the triple line) and uses DFT approximations for the grand potential.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the four types of bridging states based on pinning conditions, show surface phase diagrams detailing transitions between gas, liquid, and bridging phases, and compare theoretical predictions for the triple-point line $L_T(\delta)$.
paper_structure: The paper systematically maps out the phase diagram by analyzing different slit width regimes (e.g., $L > L_T(\delta)$ vs. $L < L_D(\delta)$) under varying shear conditions, deriving specific equations for phase boundaries for each transition type.
why_interesting: The study of confined fluids and wetting transitions, especially when coupled with external fields like shear, provides a rich playground for testing theories of phase transitions and interfacial physics, which share conceptual links with many-body systems in external potentials.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. A patterned slit of width L with alternating stripes of competing wettability, A (orange) and B (gray), each of width H, laterally displaced by δ. (a) Type I bridging: both menisci are pinned at the patch edges and meet the walls at edge contact angles θe and θ′ e = θe −2α. (b) Type IIA bridging for p < psat: one end of the meniscus is pinned and the other is unpinned meeting patch A with contact angle θ, so that the bridge covers only a length d ≤H. (c) Type-IIB bridging, for p > psat, where the unpinned end meets patch B at angle π −θ. (d) Type III, for p = psat, where the menisci are planar whose ends are unpinned and meet patch A at contact angle θ and patch B at contact angle π...

FIG. 2. Sections of the surface phase diagram showing the phase boundaries separating the stability of the capillary gas (CG), capillary liquid (CL), pinned (type I), and partially pinned (type IIA, B) bridging phases, for different slit widths and pressures: a) maximum contrast b) partial contrast with δ < δ†, c) partial contrast with δ > δ†. For partial contrast, and only at δp = 0, the bridging phases are of type III and the menisci can freely slide until they meet an AB boundary.

FIG. 3. Three dimensional phase diagrams showing the surfaces of first-order CG→CL (blue), CG→type I bridge (red) and CG →type IIA (yellow) bridge phases for maximum and partial contrast. The green line is the crossover between type I and type IIA bridging phases. At δp = 0, three-phase coexistence occurs along the orange and black lines between CG, CL and type I and type III bridging phases, respectively. Left: maximum contrast slit (θ = 0); right: partial contrast slit (θ = 30◦).

FIG. 4. DFT equilibrium density profiles for a maximum contrast slit with H = 50 σ, L = 20 σ and increasing shear displace- ments. Each of the these bridging states coexist with a CG phase. For δ = 0, 15, and 45 σ the bridging is of type I involving pinned menisci. For the intermediate shear with δ = 30 σ, the bridging phase is of type II, and only one end is pinned. For the largest shear with δ = 45 σ which corresponds to the triple point where CG, CL and type I bridge coexist, the menisci remain strongly curved, even though the pressure is very close to bulk saturation demonstrating deviations from the macroscopic expectation due to the influence of intermolecular forces.

FIG. 5. Triple-point line LT (δ) for the maximum contrast case (θ = 0) showing the comparison between the macro- scopic, mesoscopic and microscopic DFT results. Mesoscopic results account for long-ranged intermolecular forces which af- fect the surface free-energy of wetting drops and drying bub- bles on the A and B patches.
